question: What is the primary function of sensory nerves in the peripheral nervous system?

options.A: Regulating hormone release within endocrine organs
options.B: Generating voluntary motor movements in skeletal muscles
options.C: Transmitting impulses from receptors to the central nervous system
options.D: Carrying signals away from the brain

explanation: Sensory nerves are classified as afferent fibers, meaning their main job is carrying environmental and internal data toward the brain and spinal cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h1)

question: A patient with long-standing diabetes cannot feel heat in their feet. Which part of the nervous system is directly failing?
explanation: Damage to peripheral sensory nerve fibers prevents the transmission of thermal signals from the foot receptors up to the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h1)

question: Where are the cell bodies of primary sensory neurons typically located?

options.B: Anterior horn of the spinal cord

explanation: Primary sensory neurons have their cell bodies clustered in the dorsal root ganglia just outside the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h2)

question: Why do myelinated sensory fibers conduct nerve impulses faster than unmyelinated ones?

options.A: Myelin allows the action potential to jump between nodes of Ranvier
options.B: Myelinated fibers do not require sodium ions for depolarization
options.C: Myelin increases the total diameter of the nerve cell body
options.D: Myelin produces continuous chemical neurotransmitters along the axon

explanation: Saltatory conduction enables the electrical impulse to leap efficiently down myelinated axons, drastically speeding up transmission time. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h2)

question: Which sensory receptor type responds specifically to tissue damage and extreme temperatures?
explanation: Nociceptors are specialized free nerve endings that signal actual or potential tissue damage, perceived as pain. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h3)

question: A nurse touches a patient's skin with a tuning fork to test vibration sense. Which receptor is being stimulated?
explanation: Mechanoreceptors detect mechanical displacement forces such as touch, pressure, vibration, and stretch. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h3)

question: What is the term for converting an environmental stimulus into a cellular electrical signal?
explanation: Sensory transduction is the exact process where physical or chemical stimuli are transformed into electrical membrane potentials. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h4)

question: How does a sensory nerve fiber signal a stronger stimulus to the brain?

options.A: By changing the chemical type of the electrical charge
options.B: By widening the physical diameter of the nerve axon
options.C: By releasing larger individual neurotransmitter molecules
options.D: By increasing the frequency of emitted action potentials

explanation: Nerve fibers encode stimulus strength through the rate or frequency of action potential firing rather than changing action potential size. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h4)

question: Which brain structure acts as the major relay station for ascending sensory information before it reaches the cortex?
explanation: The thalamus processes and routes almost all incoming sensory signals to the correct areas of the cerebral cortex. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h5)

question: A stroke affecting the right cerebral cortex causes sensory loss on which side of the body?
explanation: Ascending sensory pathways cross over to the opposite side of the nervous system, meaning the right cerebral hemisphere receives input from the left side of the body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h5)

question: Where is the primary somatosensory cortex located in the human brain?

options.C: Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
options.D: Precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe

explanation: The primary somatosensory cortex is situated in the postcentral gyrus, directly behind the central sulcus in the parietal lobe. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h6)

question: Why do the fingers and lips occupy a much larger area on the brain's sensory map than the back?

options.A: They are located closer to the spinal cord pathways
options.B: They require more blood flow to maintain basic muscle tone
options.C: They contain a significantly higher density of sensory receptors
options.D: They receive third-order neurons from the cerebellum

explanation: Cortical representation size is directly proportional to the density of peripheral sensory receptors in that body part. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h6)

question: Which nursing tool is best suited for assessing vibration sense during a neurological examination?
explanation: A vibrating tuning fork placed on bony prominences evaluates the integrity of deep mechanoreceptors and posterior spinal columns. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h7)

question: What does a nurse document when a patient completely loses all ability to feel pain?
explanation: Anesthesia refers to the complete loss of sensation, whereas paresthesia describes abnormal tingling sensations. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h7)
